name: Fridericianum
watch: A 2025 Marisa Merz show was cancelled over the funders' post-documenta code of conduct.
why_flagged: A 2025 Marisa Merz show was cancelled over the funders' post-documenta code of conduct.
records_note: Its imprint names the city of Kassel and Hesse as owners.
affiliations_note: Run by documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH, the same non-profit company that stages documenta; the City of Kassel and State of Hesse are its shareholders. Member of Deutscher Museumsbund, Gallery Climate Coalition.

overview: Kunsthalle for contemporary art at Friedrichsplatz 18 in central Kassel, and the central venue of documenta since the first edition in 1955 (Wikipedia).

Completed in 1779 for Landgrave Friedrich II to show the landgraves' art collections. German Wikipedia calls it "eines der ersten öffentlichen Kunstmuseen auf dem europäischen Kontinent". A Kunsthalle since 1988, opened by Veit Loers (Wikipedia).
Architect Simon Louis du Ry. It served as the Westphalian estates' palace from 1810 to 1813, and its library burned in a bombing raid in September 1941 with about 350,000 volumes lost (Wikipedia).
Directors have included René Block, Rein Wolfs and Susanne Pfeffer. Moritz Wesseler has led it since November 2018 (Wikipedia).
Programme in 2026 includes interventions by Raque Ford, Karl Holmqvist and Kerstin Brätsch (stated by the space).
Visiting: Tuesday to Sunday and public holidays 11 am to 6 pm, Thursday to 8 pm (stated by the space).
details.funding_verdict: Fridericianum: public: the City of Kassel and the State of Hesse in equal shares, through documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH
funding: The building is owned by the State of Hesse and run by documenta und Museum Fridericianum gGmbH (Wikipedia).
That company is "funded to an equal extent by the City of Kassel and the State of Hesse" (documenta Code of Conduct). Its managing director is Andreas Hoffmann (Monopol).

red_flags.heading: Show cancelled over the documenta code of conduct (2025)
points: After the antisemitism scandal at documenta fifteen, documenta and the Fridericianum adopted a Code of Conduct, posted in February 2025, that treats the IHRA working definition of antisemitism as binding (Monopol; documenta; ArtAsiaPacific).
The code lets documenta step in if the supervisory board finds "artistic forms of expression to be in conflict with [its] principles" (ArtAsiaPacific).

A Marisa Merz exhibition planned from late August 2025 to January 2026 did not take place: the Fondazione Merz withdrew because its president Beatrice Merz does not fully agree with the IHRA definition and preferred the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism (Monopol, 4 December 2025).
Beatrice Merz: "Ich bin der Überzeugung, dass Kunst nicht durch Grenzen eingeschränkt werden sollte" (Monopol).

Hoffmann said the framework "was not entirely compatible" and the code binds staff but not the artistic team or outsiders; works by Robert Grosvenor and Portia Zvavahera were shown instead (Monopol). Finestre sull'Arte quotes Hoffmann saying the framework was "not entirely compatible".

press.overall: The criticism is of the documenta code of conduct that governs the Fridericianum, not of its programme; the one case that names it is the Merz withdrawal.

items.title: editorial staff, "Ausstellung in Kassel wegen Code of Conduct der Documenta abgesagt" (2025)
points: Reports the Merz withdrawal and Hoffmann's answer; names the Fridericianum.

items.title: editorial staff, "Germany, skips Marisa Merz exhibition: disagreement over definition of anti-Semitism" (2025)
points: Notes the IHRA definition is disputed because it can classify protests against the Israeli government as antisemitic.

items.title: Adam Broomberg, "The Twisted Logic of Documenta's 'Artistic Freedom'" (2025)
points: Argues the IHRA-based code makes curating "the execution of omission" and that the only path with integrity is to boycott these institutions.
Does not name the Fridericianum.

wider_context: ArtAsiaPacific (2025) reported that critics denounced the code, worried it could be used to suppress pro-Palestinian artists.
The Fridericianum is run by the same company and bound by the same code, which is how the Merz show fell through.
details.bottom_line: The money is public: the City of Kassel and the State of Hesse fund the company that runs it, with no private sponsor on record. The weak point is political control through the documenta code of conduct, which cost it the Marisa Merz show in 2025. Worth watching: whether other artists or lenders withdraw over the code, and documenta 16.

name: GfZK, Galerie für Zeitgenössische Kunst Leipzig
funding: In 2016 the Stiftung GfZK was funded by the city of Leipzig, the Saxon science and arts ministry and the Förderkreis of the gallery at 220,000 euros a year each (Saxon ministry release, 8 February 2016). In June 2025 the Greens' Claudia Maicher criticised Saxon budget draft cuts that include the GfZK (L-IZ, 1 June 2025).
watch: A gallery of contemporary art in Leipzig, with Franciska Zólyom as director since 1 January 2012 and her contract extended from 2017 for five years (Saxon ministry release, 8 February 2016).
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts; the 2016 ministry release gives the shares of the three funders.

overview: The GfZK is a gallery of contemporary art at Karl-Tauchnitz-Straße 9 to 11, Leipzig (gallery website).

It is run by a foundation whose council extended Franciska Zólyom's contract as director for five years from 1 January 2017; she has led it since 1 January 2012 (Saxon ministry release, 8 February 2016).
What is there: temporary exhibitions; the site lists a library as one of its locations but the pages read gave no holdings or collection size (gallery website).
Archive: the site's Archive link refers to past exhibitions (gallery website).
details.funding_verdict: GfZK: three equal funders, the city of Leipzig, the Saxon state and the gallery's friends' circle (2016 figures).
funding: City of Leipzig: 220,000 euros a year (Saxon ministry release, 8 February 2016).
No later budget found on the pages read.

red_flags.heading: Funding cut
points: Die Leipziger Internet Zeitung, 1 June 2025: Claudia Maicher (Greens) said the Saxon government's budget draft cuts also affect the GfZK, with a lawnmower approach and no visible concept; the article gives no GfZK amount and no reply from the culture ministry.

details.bottom_line: In 2016 the funding was split into three equal parts: city, state and friends. The 2025 budget cuts reach it; the pages read do not give the amount.

name: Glyptothek
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the Glyptothek or give amounts. Its own history page says King Ludwig I paid for both the building and the collection himself.
watch: Munich's museum of Greek and Roman sculpture, built by Leo von Klenze between 1816 and 1830 for Ludwig I and part of the Antike am Königsplatz group of the State Collections of Antiquities (museum website). Reopened in 1972 after bomb damage in 1944.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts or annual report.

overview: The Glyptothek is a museum of ancient sculpture at Königsplatz 3, Munich, in a building by Leo von Klenze (museum website).

Klenze built it between 1816 and 1830 as court architect to Ludwig I, who is named as its founder and benefactor; it closed at the outbreak of the Second World War, was damaged by bombing in 1944 and reopened in 1972 after reconstruction (museum website).

What is there: Greek and Roman marble sculpture from the Archaic period to Late Antiquity. Highlights listed are the Aegina pediment sculptures from the Temple of Aphaia, acquired in 1812, and the Barberini Faun, a Hellenistic work of about 220 B.C. The museum calls itself the only museum in the world dedicated exclusively to ancient sculpture. The pages read gave no object count (museum website).
The collection was assembled with Johann Martin von Wagner, Ludwig's Roman art agent, and Ludwig bought the antiquities himself (museum website).
The site belongs to Antike am Königsplatz, which also runs the State Collections of Antiquities, the Pompejanum in Aschaffenburg and the Ceramics Museum Weiden (museum website).
details.funding_verdict: Glyptothek: funder not stated on the pages read; founded and first paid for by a king.
funding: Founding: Ludwig I paid for the collection and the building himself (museum website, history page).
Current funding: the pages read did not state the funder, a budget or sponsors.
details.bottom_line: The pages read name no sponsor and no budget, so who pays today stays open here. The founding money was a monarch's own. Check the Bavarian state budget for the State Collections of Antiquities.

name: Haus der Kulturen der Welt (HKW)
funding: Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media (BKM), Auswärtiges Amt.
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.

overview: Venue for international contemporary arts and debate in the former Kongresshalle on the Spree in the Grosser Tiergarten, Berlin. The HKW has used the building since 1989 (German Wikipedia).

The American architect Hugh Stubbins designed the Kongresshalle for the 1957 Interbau building exhibition, as a gift from the United States. Berliners nicknamed it the "pregnant oyster" (Wikipedia, German Wikipedia).
The grounds were earlier the site of Magnus Hirschfeld's Institut für Sexualwissenschaft (Wikipedia).

Part of the roof collapsed on 21 May 1980, killing a Sender Freies Berlin radio journalist. The hall was rebuilt in its original style and reopened in 1987 (Wikipedia). A partial restoration was completed in 2019 (German Wikipedia).
Run by Kulturveranstaltungen des Bundes in Berlin GmbH (German Wikipedia).
Bernd M. Scherer led the house from 2006. Bonaventure Soh Bejeng Ndikung became director on 1 January 2023 (German Wikipedia).

Work is organised in three areas: literature, society and science. Visual arts and film. Music and performing arts. Since 2013 it has run multi-year projects including the Anthropozän-Projekt, "100 Jahre Gegenwart" and "Das Neue Alphabet" (German Wikipedia).
details.funding_verdict: HKW: mainly public: German federal government
funding: Regular funding comes from the Federal Commissioner for Culture and the Media (BKM) and the Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt) (German Wikipedia). English Wikipedia names HKW as one of the federal "lighthouses of culture" funded by the federal culture minister and the Federal Foreign Office.
Hyperallergic's Adam Broomberg writes that HKW "is funded almost entirely by the federal government" (Hyperallergic, 5 November 2025).

red_flags.heading: State censorship or punishment, concert cancelled after the federal culture minister's call
points: Funder: the federal culture minister's office (BKM) is one of HKW's two regular funders (German Wikipedia).

Federal culture minister Wolfram Weimer sharply criticised the appearance of the rapper Chefket, planned for 7 October 2025 at HKW as part of Jan Böhmermann's exhibition "Die Möglichkeit der Unvernunft" (title translated: "The Possibility of Unreason"). He objected to a T-shirt Chefket wears in photos, showing a map of Palestine without Israel, which the federal government considers antisemitic, and called on the HKW director to intervene (Jüdische Allgemeine, dpa, 29 September 2025).
The HKW director had earlier pointed to Böhmermann's artistic freedom and clear stance on antisemitism (Jüdische Allgemeine).

Cancellation: on 29 September 2025 the organisers, listed in the statement as Böhmermann, his group Royale and HKW as venue, announced that the 7 October event was cancelled. The statement says "Diesen Einspruch nehmen wir ernst" (translated: "We take this objection seriously") and gives it as the reason for cancelling (Jüdische Allgemeine).

press.overall: One piece in the art press argues that HKW's federal funding brings state control, and criticises the handling of Gaza under the Ndikung directorship.

items.title: Adam Broomberg, "The Irony of a Fascism Exhibition in Germany" (5 November 2025)
points: Argues the HKW, "once a custodian of critical culture", has become "a model of capitulation to state control", and that its near-total federal funding "has a price: preemptive obedience".
Says Ndikung's appointment came with the condition that he publicly renounce the BDS movement, which he did in 2022 (Broomberg's claim).

Criticises the exhibition "Global Fascisms" ("Not one work in the exhibition acknowledges the world burning just beyond the door") and calls Roee Rosen's "Gaza War Tattoos" an aestheticisation of atrocity.
Does not mention Weimer or Böhmermann.

wider_context: 2022 appointment: the federal government's antisemitism commissioner Felix Klein and the Israeli ambassador Ron Prosor criticised the incoming director Ndikung in papers of the Funke Mediengruppe and accused him of closeness to the BDS movement. Ndikung said "Ich habe die BDS-Bewegung nicht unterstützt und unterstütze sie auch heute nicht." Culture minister Claudia Roth said she had no objection to the procedure or its result (Jüdische Allgemeine, dpa, 28 October 2022).
Roth said she was not involved in the selection, which fell in the term of her predecessor Monika Grütters (Jüdische Allgemeine).
Ndikung took office at HKW on 1 January 2023.
details.bottom_line: HKW is paid for by the German federal government through the culture commissioner's office and the Foreign Office. The documented weak point is political pressure on its programme: the federal culture minister's call to the director over the Chefket concert, cancelled on 29 September 2025 by the organisers including HKW, and the 2022 accusations against its incoming director from the federal antisemitism commissioner and the Israeli ambassador.

name: Julia Stoschek Foundation (Julia Stoschek Collection / JSC Berlin)

overview: Private foundation showing the Julia Stoschek Collection of time-based media art, with a Berlin venue on Leipziger Strasse and a venue in Düsseldorf (USA Art News, 2026; Apollo, 2016).
Julia Stoschek opened the Düsseldorf venue to the public in 2007 and the Berlin venue in June 2016 (USA Art News; Apollo).
The collection holds more than 850 works by about 250 artists, mostly European and American, from the 1960s onward, including video, internet-based works and performance (Wikipedia).

Berlin building: the former Czech Cultural Centre, a GDR-era building of 3,000 square metres (USA Art News; Apollo). Düsseldorf is a converted industrial building from 1907 with a cinema and an archive (Apollo).

Berlin ran about 22 exhibitions and drew roughly 450,000 visitors. On 24 April 2026 USA Art News reported that the foundation will close the Berlin venue at the end of October 2026 and keep Düsseldorf open, with more international presentations of the collection.
details.funding_verdict: Julia Stoschek Foundation: private foundation of collector Julia Stoschek; no source opened says how it is financed
funding: W Magazine (Diane Solway, 20 November 2017) says Stoschek is "an active shareholder" in her family's auto-parts company Brose, whose chairman is her father Michael Stoschek. It does not say how the collection is financed.
Brose reported sales of €7.7 billion for 2024 (Wikipedia).

press.overall: The Brose items are newspaper pieces, listed under Wider context.

wider_context: Brose was founded in Coburg on 14 June 1919 by Max Brose and Ernst Jühling. Max Brose joined the Nazi Party in 1933. In the Second World War the company made gasoline canisters and armaments for the military and used forced labour, including prisoners of war (Wikipedia). Julia Stoschek is Max Brose's great-granddaughter (Tagesspiegel headline; Berliner Zeitung).
The company and family say Max Brose treated workers well; Wikipedia states that claim "has not been substantiated".

Tagesspiegel, Nicola Kuhn, "Die Sammlerin Julia Stoschek und ihr Urgroßvater: Schmutzige Gelder, saubere Kunst" (11 November 2020; paywalled, only excerpts were read): the artist Leon Kahane showed an installation near the Julia Stoschek Collection on Leipziger Strasse during the Art Week, referring to Brose's ties to the armaments industry under National Socialism. The teaser (my translation) says forced labour keeps coming up, also in the cultural sector, and that ducking the issue does not help. The excerpt does not say whether Brose money funds the collection.

Berliner Zeitung, Hanno Hauenstein, "Ende der Documenta 15: Warum diese Debatte uns noch lange begleiten wird" (25 September 2022; opinion-led commentary in the culture section): the author says Stoschek shields her great-grandfather's Nazi past "aktiv gegen Kritik" (actively against criticism). The piece says the company commissioned a publication from a historian that faced criticism for missing footnotes.

Unverified: the same Berliner Zeitung piece says Michael Stoschek pressed in 2015 to rename the former Von-Schultes-Strasse as Max-Brose-Strasse and compared Brose to Oskar Schindler; that artist Hito Steyerl bought back her work from the collection shortly after David de Jong's text criticising the lack of transparency of wealthy families' Nazi ties; and that the paper received an Abmahnung (a warning letter) over a phrase in its translation of that text, which it attributes to Stoschek's side without naming a sender. How the matter ended is not reported.
The founder is an active shareholder in Brose, an auto supplier (W Magazine, 2017).
details.bottom_line: The founder is an active shareholder in Brose, an auto supplier that used forced labour in the Nazi era, and the criticism concerns that family history, not the programme. Worth watching: whether the foundation publishes its financing, and what follows the Berlin closure at the end of October 2026.

name: Lothringer 13 Halle
tier_note: No source outside the museum is recorded.
highlight: Lothringer 13 Halle is a Kulturreferat institution in a former engine-grinding workshop in Haidhausen, with about 700 square metres and free admission.

overview: Exhibition space for international and local contemporary art at Lothringer Straße 13 in Haidhausen, Munich, near Weißenburger Platz, with about 700 square metres in rotating group shows (muenchen.de).
Founded in 1980 as a Künstlerwerkstatt in a former machine factory (German Wikipedia).
The exhibition rooms are in a former engine-grinding workshop (Motorenschleiferei) in a rear building. The front building houses a space for research and information (City of Munich).
Between 1980 and 1998 the city's culture department, guest curators and staff organised the exhibitions. Since 1998 rotating independent curators have led the programme (German Wikipedia).
A second unit, Lothringer13_Florida, a collective space for interdisciplinary and media projects, was created in 2014 (German Wikipedia).
German Wikipedia states that Lisa Britzger became artistic director in 2020 and Kalas Liebfried took over as head in April 2025.

Open Wednesday to Friday 12:00 to 20:00 and Saturday and Sunday 10:00 to 18:00, closed Monday and Tuesday, and open only during a running event. Admission is free and the entrance is barrier-free (muenchen.de).
details.funding_verdict: Lothringer 13 Halle: public: run by the Kulturreferat of the city of Munich
funding: The Halle is run by the Kulturreferat of the Landeshauptstadt München, and entry to the exhibitions is free (City of Munich).
German Wikipedia states that the Halle is funded by city grants, project money and donations.
details.bottom_line: The money behind Lothringer 13 Halle is municipal: the Kulturreferat of the city of Munich runs it, and German Wikipedia lists city grants, project money and donations as its funding.

name: Museum Fünf Kontinente
funding: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or give amounts. Its history page says the Kingdom of Bavaria paid for collecting in the 19th century, and the home page links to a Preetorius-Stiftung without describing it.
watch: Munich's ethnological museum, with a first curator hired in 1862 and a public opening in 1868. Its Africa collection holds about 50 objects assigned to the Benin Empire; the museum ran provenance research on them from December 2021 to May 2022, and Die Berliner Zeitung reported on 17 May 2023 that Bavaria and Saxony were the only German states without a return contract with Nigeria.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts or annual report.

overview: Museum Fünf Kontinente is an ethnological museum at Maximilianstraße 42, Munich, in the building it moved into in 1925 and 1926 (museum website, history).

Its first curator, Moritz Wagner, was hired in 1862 when the collection belonged to the Kingdom of Bavaria; it opened to the public in 1868 in the Hofgarten arcades, was renamed Museum für Völkerkunde in 1917 and Museum Fünf Kontinente in 2014 (museum website, history). Uta Werlich has directed it since April 2018.

What is there: holdings from five centuries, still growing. The history page names Max Buchner, who brought over 4,000 artefacts, Princess Therese of Bavaria, who bequeathed almost 3,000 objects, and Christine Scherman, who gave more than 1,800 photographs. It gives no total object count (museum website, history).
Benin: about 50 objects in the Africa collection are assigned to the Benin Empire or marked Benin City in the entry books (German Lost Art Foundation page on the museum's Benin collections).

Archive: the library holds over 100,000 volumes and 120 periodicals, is a public reading library and is open Tuesday to Thursday 9:30 to 13:00 and 14:00 to 17:30 and Friday 9:30 to 13:00; the page does not mention an archive or photo archive (museum website, library). Online collection database: onlinedatenbank-museum-fuenf-kontinente.de.
details.funding_verdict: Museum Fünf Kontinente: funder not stated on the pages read; 19th-century collecting was paid by the Kingdom of Bavaria.
funding: Historic funder: the Kingdom of Bavaria funded collecting in the 19th century (museum website, history).
Today: the pages read did not state the funder, a budget or sponsors. The home page links a Preetorius-Stiftung without saying what it does.

red_flags.heading: Looted or contested holdings
points: The museum ran a provenance research project from 1 December 2021 to May 2022, planned for four months and extended to six, on objects that entered the collection from 1898 onward, to test links to the British punitive expedition of 1897 or other violent appropriation (German Lost Art Foundation).
The page says the vast majority of the objects had no fully clarified provenance before the project and does not report findings or a return (German Lost Art Foundation).
Die Berliner Zeitung, 17 May 2023: Bavaria and Saxony were the only two German states that had not concluded return contracts with Nigeria. The article gives no Bavarian statement.

The museum's history page says it returned a Chinese artwork to the Bernheimer family in 1949 and that current debates prompt it to re-examine its colonial past; it lists no colonial-era returns (museum website, history).

details.bottom_line: The pages read do not say who pays for the museum today, which is the main gap. What is contested is the Benin holding: about 50 objects, researched in 2021 and 2022, with no return reported on the pages read.

name: Museum MMK für Moderne Kunst
funding: A museum of the City of Frankfurt am Main (museumsufer.de); its contact address is a city address. The pages read did not state amounts or name sponsors.
watch: The city's museum of art from the 1960s to today, in a 1991 building by Hans Hollein with two further sites, ZOLLAMT and TOWER; museumsufer.de lists the main building as closed for fire-safety renovation. In 2022 about 80 per cent of staff signed an anonymous letter to director Susanne Pfeffer describing a toxic work culture (ArtReview, 18 May 2022), and in May 2023 the city's culture department told the city assembly that a mediation had been declared failed by staff.
records_note: The pages read did not show published accounts; as a city museum its money sits in the City of Frankfurt budget.

overview: A museum of modern and contemporary art in Frankfurt am Main with three sites: the main building at Domstraße 10, ZOLLAMT MMK at Domstraße 3 and TOWER MMK near the Bahnhofsviertel (museumsufer.de).

The main building was erected in 1991 to a design by the Vienna architect Hans Hollein; it is 'a museum of the City of Frankfurt am Main' (museumsufer.de). Susanne Pfeffer is director (ArtReview, 18 May 2022).

The collection holds more than 5,000 works from the 1960s to the present, with central groups of works by international and national artists (museumsufer.de). The pages read did not state where the founding holdings came from.
The main building is listed as closed for fire-safety renovation (museumsufer.de, read 14 November 2026).
details.funding_verdict: Museum MMK für Moderne Kunst: public, a museum of the City of Frankfurt; amounts not stated on the pages read
funding: City of Frankfurt am Main: the museum is a city museum (museumsufer.de) and uses a city e-mail address (MMK website). The pages read did not state the budget.
No reporting found of named sponsors or foundation amounts on the pages read.

red_flags.heading: Labour dispute
points: ArtReview reported on 18 May 2022 that about 80 per cent of employees anonymously signed a six-page letter to director Susanne Pfeffer describing a toxic, abusive work culture, repeated boundary violations and opaque decisions; the letter was seen by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung. A first letter in 2019 raised similar concerns.
The second letter was sent on 5 April 2022 with a 14-day deadline and was made public when management did not reply in time (ArtReview, 18 May 2022).
Reply: Pfeffer told the FAZ she issued an internal response on 13 May 2022 setting out 'significant structural reforms' (ArtReview, 18 May 2022).

At the city assembly's question time on 11 May 2023 a CDU member said staff had declared the mediation that followed 'failed'; culture councillor Ina Hartwig answered that the Magistrat intends 'to go new ways' to improve structures with all involved and that its duty of care covers both staff and management (City of Frankfurt, Dezernat Kultur und Wissenschaft, answer to question 1652).

details.bottom_line: The city pays; no figures or sponsors were on the pages read. The open matter is the staff complaint about management, raised in 2019 and 2022 and still before the city assembly in May 2023.

name: Residenztheater (Bayerisches Staatsschauspiel)
funding: The Bayerisches Staatsschauspiel is a Bavarian state theatre; the Free State of Bavaria is funding a new rehearsal and workshop centre for it with a total budget of roughly EUR 196 million (Bavarian building ministry, 2024).
watch: The Staatsschauspiel plays at the Residenztheater, the Marstall and the Cuvilliéstheater. Its new production centre in Bogenhausen was topped out in December 2024, with completion planned for December 2026.
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts.

overview: The Bayerisches Staatsschauspiel performs at the Residenztheater, the Marstall and the Cuvilliéstheater in Munich (Bavarian building ministry, 2024).
The pages read did not state the founding year or the Intendant.

What is there: a German-language repertory with English surtitles on some productions; November 2026 listings include König Lear, Faust I (directed by Ulrich Rasche, a co-production with the Salzburg Festival), Cabaret and Ödipus in Robert Icke's adaptation, with an ensemble listed on the site (theatre website).

The new Bogenhausen centre will house the production workshops and three rehearsal stages on about 12,500 square metres, consolidating operations now spread across the city (Bavarian building ministry, 2024).
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive.
details.funding_verdict: Residenztheater: public, paid for by the Free State of Bavaria; operating subsidy not stated on the pages read
funding: Free State of Bavaria: total budget of roughly EUR 196 million for the new rehearsal and workshop centre; groundbreaking June 2023, topping-out December 2024, completion planned December 2026. Staatliches Bauamt Regensburg oversees it and Implenia Hochbau GmbH is general contractor (Bavarian building ministry press release, 2024).
No reporting found of the operating subsidy or earned income on the pages read.
details.bottom_line: The Free State of Bavaria pays; the pages read give a capital figure of about EUR 196 million but no operating subsidy. No controversy was found on the pages read.

name: Schinkel Pavillon
funding: Run by the association Schinkel Pavillon e.V.; the pages read did not name its funders. In December 2024 ArtDog Istanbul reported the space said it could lose 50% of its funding under a proposed 13% cut to Berlin arts funding of about 130 million euros.
watch: An octagonal building in Oberwallstraße designed by the East German architect Richard Paulick, hosting non-commercial exhibitions run by the Kunstverein Schinkel Pavillon e.V. since 2007 (Berliner Zeitung, 27 November 2024).
records_note: The pages read gave no accounts; the association is a registered Verein.

overview: The Schinkel Pavillon is an octagonal exhibition building in Oberwallstraße, Berlin (Berliner Zeitung, 27 November 2024).
It was designed by the East German architect Richard Paulick; since 2007 the Kunstverein Schinkel Pavillon e.V. has run non-commercial exhibitions there (Berliner Zeitung, 27 November 2024).
What is there: temporary exhibitions of contemporary art; the pages read describe no permanent collection.
Archive: the pages read did not describe an archive. The space's own site loaded only as a blank page on 2026-11-18.
details.funding_verdict: Schinkel Pavillon: mainly public Berlin funding, funders not named on the pages read; at risk from Berlin's 2025 cuts.
funding: The pages read did not name the funders. ArtDog Istanbul, 10 December 2024: the Pavillon announced it could lose 50% of its funding and may close permanently.
Context: Berlin proposed a 13% cut to arts funding, about 130 million euros, while arts funding makes up just over 2% of the city budget (ArtDog Istanbul, 10 December 2024).

red_flags.heading: Funding cut
points: Berliner Zeitung, 27 November 2024: a commentary by Ingeborg Ruthe asked whether the Pavillon would soon be cut to the bone and said art associations seem to have no political lobby; no amounts or Senate reply were given.

ArtDog Istanbul, 10 December 2024: KW Institute, Künstlerhaus Bethanien, n.b.k. and nGbK warned of a domino effect; the Berlin Museums Association called the cuts a painful burden for smaller institutions; culture senator Joe Chialo called them very drastic and brutal and said he would seek alternative solutions.

details.bottom_line: The pages read do not show who pays beyond the association; Berlin public money is the exposed part, with the space warning of a 50% loss in late 2024. Whether the cut took effect is not shown on these pages.
details.website: https://www.schinkelpavillon.de/ (checked 2026-11-18; loaded as a blank page)
